newsitem.title: USA: U.S. attache sees Taiwan beef imports up sharply.
newsitem.headline: U.S. attache sees Taiwan beef imports up sharply.

text.p: Taiwan beef imports are expected to grow signficantly in 1997 as consumers shift from pork following the March outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease among hogs on the island, a U.S. agricultural attache said.

In an annual report on Taiwan livestock dated July 21, the attache said imports of U.S. beef totaled 10,795 tonnes in 1996, up seven percent from the 1995 record level while beef imports from all other suppliers decreased.

She said U.S. market share in terms of import volume grew to 22 percent in 1996 and is expected to grow further in 1997 and 1998. U.S. market share in terms of import value hit 35 percent in 1996 and the U.S. replaced Australia as the most valuable supplier for beef.
"Some traders predict that the United States, Australia and New Zealand will each take one third of the market share at the turn of the next century," the attache wrote.
She said the negative impact of the epidemic on pork demand will likely be much less in 1998, when Taiwan's total beef imports are expected to grow three percent.
Turning to pork, the attache said Taiwan's hog production in the future was unlikely to resume the peak level -- 15 million annual output --- given new clean water rules now in place.

She also said that according to Japanese quarantine requirements, Taiwan might not be able to export pork to Japan for up to five years. Prior to the outbreak, about 40 percent of the island's pigs slaughtered for exports, mainly to Japan.
"Taiwan might lose this market forever as marketing channels and contacts are no longer valid after being absent for five years," the attache wrote.
Attache reports are not official USDA data.
